item.description:
After first hearing about Roman Sands Re:Build, and following along with bits of its development over the last few years, it's been a real ride getting to sit down with it; the demo from a couple years ago gave us a glimpse at both of the game's very different acts, a contrast that I initially misunderstood as a moving continuously back-and-forth between two realities situation (it's not). Fast forward to last night: almost fourteen hours in, Re:Build is already cementing itself in my head as one of those unclassifiable experiences that defies neat or sensible analysis and certainly isn't the sort of game that, in an ideal world, should be scored. (The "Re:Build" appendage is to distinguish this game from 2019's Roman Sands, its first iteration that was reportedly not quite cooked yet.)
Re:Build is a tonal whiplash in game form: the first act is a fiendish immersive sim drenched in a vaporwave glitchcore palette, and the second is a slow, plodding journey through what I can only describe as Evangelion survival purgatory (I am not well-versed in Eva, but know enough about it to recognise its hallmarks and signature aesthetics). Both acts prod at the abject madness it takes to stay alive, and both are set in fractured realities beset by time loops. By "staying alive," I don't mean the basics of breathing and eating, or the general duty of parenting or caregiving, but the great chaotic ballet of service, sacrifice, and maintenance that goes into keeping life as a whole going (in Singapore, we call a lot of this stuff "sai kang" – Hokkien for "shit work"). Everything is stylish as hell and the intro video goes so hard I fear that the game may not live up to the vibes, which are currently orbiting us somewhere in space.
In Act One, the player washes up on the beach of a cursed resort, where each day their sole purpose is to please its four miserable residents in increasingly optimised ways. A lot of it is indentured-servant bullshit devoid of dignity: cleaning up vomit, fetching trinkets, giving massages to joyless hags, and so on. Every day is part of a hellish sunbleached cycle, and depending on the changes and discoveries made around the resort each day, offers a slightly more optimised route to keep these awful people happy. Each morning I emerge from the waves, and each day my body becomes a machine devoted to the fine art of meeting and anticipating the master's needs; in the evening, I return to the ocean, where my performance is evaluated. Did I mention the frighteningly engorged sun hanging in the sky, poised to deliver our annihilation?
I will always admire an imsim that commits not just to pushing the player over the edge, but getting a willing player to run screaming toward the precipice all on their own. Re:Build's first act is a masterclass in doing exactly that, if you have the constitution and mental resilience for the (brilliantly designed) busywork. I've had my share of service jobs, and owned-and-operated a couple of brick-and-mortar businesses that occasionally involved picking up human faeces (not part of the job description). Re:Build expertly reproduces a very specific sort of service work – the endless layers of exploitation and mental gymnastics, the gradual feeling of lulling yourself into a speedy productive rhythm, the poisoned high of performing the most banal, demeaning tasks for people who couldn't care if you were alive or dead.
Video games and capitalism prepared me well for this moment; there is nothing like chasing the stupid high of checking off silly little tasks for little to no reward (it's all mostly cosmetics and gacha, and occasionally a key item to move the story along). Every time I move between areas eats up a block of precious time, and the residents move around to different locations as the day goes on. I develop pathetic, affectionate pity for Bunk, the pervy writer who spends all day getting tanked, throwing up, and hitting on Sylvia; the latter is an evasive manipulative sort who would almost certainly find a way to make the trolley problem worse. Betty and Harold are the old couple from hell, a two-headed moral justification for euthanasia.
And then I meet Kara, my mysterious chain-smoking coworker who actually knows what the island is – we're trapped, apparently, in the decaying dream of an angel – and how to set ourselves free. I spend almost six hours ranking up to level 31+ in Act One, chugging along even when I become braindead and frustrated, promising myself that the next day will be better, that I'll finally complete the puzzles I'm working on between making negronis and fetching towels. The thing is, I have all the tools I need at this point, but committing myself to a real solution is to leave behind my toxic but familiar little miseries.
Oh right, the puzzles. You almost forget you're there to get off the damn island before the sun goes sideways. There are three big ones to solve around the resort, sort of in the tradition of Myst, and a couple of them are trickier than they look; there's no overt signposting for the solutions besides common sense (for instance, it's pretty easy to see a link between the orrery in the courtyard, and another similar planetary display inside the resort) or trial-and-error shenanigans. Depending how distracted you get by the residents' parasitical need for your attention, the puzzles can be solved pretty easily once you have all the requisite items. At times, the UI design wasn't as clear as it could be, and doing the orrery puzzle on a controller was nightmarish (it was fine once I switched to the keyboard and mouse).
My biggest pain point is Act Two, when we get to the real sad-sack heart of Re:Build: my cow has died, and I have to move around her dead body and stare at her lifeless face while I get my bearings. I've just woken up in some kind of sealed, failing zoological research station, and there's a parasite on board interfering with critical systems. Kara is here too (or at least, someone who looks just like her and knows me), talking to me over some kind of communication network, but she isn't wildly helpful, and I have to move around the station managing oxygen flow so that I can handle the aforementioned parasite before I share the same fate as my poor cow. After Act One, the atmosphere here is a bit like ducking underwater into thick, oppressive isolation – just the sound of my footsteps and the station's creaky sounds of protest as I cluelessly try to poke at various valves and gears.
There's a lot to unpack here on several levels for Evangelion fans, especially because the in-game interfaces around the station are clear little homages to the very distinct NERV supercomputers, through their iconic bicolor graphical displays that almost singlehandedly keep Tumblr going. There's also a lot to unpack with how, after exploring enough in the station to thread together the connections to the resort, both acts are strange cousins from the same nightmarish tree. Act Two is appropriately punishing for a lot of reasons, but there is nothing "fun" about pushing through Act One either. It is a marathon of masochism that I've willingly signed up for, hungry for the little microdoses of serotonin along the way, snug in the false intimacy I've developed with the residents. The drum-n-bass soundtrack is diabolically good, too – frenetic breakbeats are the perfect, peristaltic sonic accompaniment to keep me going. Act Two, though, has the same vibes as the imploded billionaire submersible: bleak as hell, undeniably stressful, and heading towards an increasingly palpable but unknowable doom.
I am not good at figuring out doohickeys and cranks and mechanical bits, which is why I will be the first to die in a crisis. I'm okay with that. In Act Two, you have a lot of these things around you – valves and buttons and little levers? I think they're levers? Things you can manipulate with tools – a screwdriver, wrench, and even a PDA that gives you abstract Ikea-like information about all the broken equipment that defies logical touch. I fiddle with all of the doodads, without a thought in my head, because I left my brain and body juice behind in Act One. I pick up clumps of garbage for no other reason other than it feels right to have a tidy environment to die in. I am not sure if I'm doing the right thing, directing air the right way, or pressurizing the right rooms, but it's a cyclical world, so I have nothing to lose except my waning scraps of morale. All I know is that I must enact a process called sublimation, and if I fail or pass out, I will simply wake up in the dorm section, surrounded by all the little gacha toys from Act One. It's a lovely closed loop of quiet, iterative horror, but the pace takes its toll on me quickly.
I would be lying if I said I didn't hit a wall several times in the game, in both acts. Existential despair is a hell of a drug. But so are gacha games, and the unlikely combination of gacha-imsim-puzzle genres feels inexplicable until you see it in action and know that sweet frisson of psychological radiance whenever you get a little reward. The general tone is not far removed from the most diminished husk of a person you know, who communicates through droll quips and dark humour, like some kind of existential terrorist. Act Two, set in the sunless depths of a submerged research facility, is a deliberate sensory deprivation of all the pleasant little chimes and juicy clicks and animations that propelled me forward in the resort. Here, I am surrounded by gloom and stagnation, and my only chance at life is to court death. I smoked for almost 15 years and quit in my early 30s, and at times that felt less grim than my worst hours spent stuck in Act Two.
Re:Build will ask a lot from you as a player, and it is extremely not-for-everybody, but Act Two was exceptionally not for me. I do not wish to come back here, which is, considering its setting is a psychological horror deathtrap, a heartfelt compliment to the devs. It is, however, a critical narrative companion to Act One, and for all its misery, should not be waved away as the "less engaging" or "more draggy" section for the sake of ease. Each act riffs on the other to explore the nature of keeping ourselves and others alive, and maintaining life (or failing) at the expense of our own. Both are two sides of a profoundly dense coin, and can only be fully understood as a pair.
The price may be your sanity, intense overthinking about the flesh that houses your consciousness, and maybe some time spent looking up how to troubleshoot a few bugs. But in return, Roman Sands Re:Build will do the important and underappreciated work of clamping your eyelids open to face the uncomfortable intricacies of living, keeping life going, and the rituals we develop to maintain our realities. I'd just prefer one in which my cow makes it out alive.
A copy of Roman Sands Re:Build was provided for this review by Serenity Forge.

item.title: Tim Schafer - the founder of acclaimed developer Double Fine Productions, and the legendary designer behind the likes of Day of the Tentacle and Psychonauts - has spoken out about his studio's recent shift to independence, as well as Game Pass, and industry woes at large. Read more
item.description:
Tim Schafer - the founder of acclaimed developer Double Fine Productions, and the legendary designer behind the likes of Day of the Tentacle and Psychonauts - has spoken out about his studio's recent shift to independence, as well as Game Pass, and industry woes at large.
In an interview with the BBC, Schafer was asked what changes at Xbox had, to his mind, resulted in Microsoft jettisoning his San Francisco-based studio. "Our mission in the beginning - seven years ago - was to really support Game Pass and fill it with as much goodness as we could," he replied. "We put our back catalogue and new stuff, about 13 games on Game Pass.
Their model I think is changing. They're going in a different direction with fewer, larger IPs. So our technique of making a lot of little IPs isn't aligned with that. We wanted to keep doing that, so we went our separate ways."
When asked what he thought about Game Pass now, and the subscription service's sustainability, Schafer said: "I love it as an idea. I liked it for Double Fine games. If you're sitting in a store and holding a disc, and it costs $70, and it's about a walking lighthouse, there's a barrier there. But if you've just got to download a game you've already paid for, it might lead people to trying weird games like Double Fine makes. So I'm very pro Game Pass, and hope it succeeds and goes forward."
Schafer went on to praise Xbox's support for Double Fine while it was still part of Microsoft, saying the company "let us completely be ourselves", and enabled Double Fine to "be a bigger version of ourselves." He also emphasised he had no regrets about partnering with Xbox at the time, so it seems as though there's little ill will there.
As for Schafer's thoughts on the industry at large, he told the BBC "I don't understand the economics of making games. For years I understood them because there are layoffs - which are bad - and then the executives realise, 'Oh we fired everybody, we need someone to make this game!'. Then they hire people back.
"So I assumed there was a cycle of ups and downs, but it's been down for four years and I don't know why. I really don't because people are playing games, people are making money, so I don't know why there is a big loss of jobs. I assume someone is being greedy somewhere."
Still, Schafer has some optimism. "I hope it is a cycle and it bounces back," he said. "There's a lot of life, excitement, and creativity in the games industry now, especially in the indie space. I'm not one of those snobs who says only indie games are creative, I think a lot of triple-A games do a lot of great creative work, it's just been a much more violent place to work."
As of writing, Double Fine is in the midst of Amnesia Fortnite, a game jam in which its team creates four smaller-scope games. This year, these projects have been voted on by the public via Kickstarter, and include a city builder where structures move like giant robots and fight monsters, and a co-operative multiplayer bar crawl dungeon-crawler called Bard Crawl.

item.title: In an unusual move, developer id Software's free-to-play shooter Quake Champions is transitioning into a paid product, eight years after its original release. As part of the same move, the Microsoft studio is killing off the Microsoft Store version, meaning it's now only available on Steam. Read more
item.description:
In an unusual move, developer id Software's free-to-play shooter Quake Champions is transitioning into a paid product, eight years after its original release. As part of the same move, the Microsoft studio is killing off the Microsoft Store version, meaning it's now only available on Steam.
Quake Champions' new paid version costs £8.99/$9.99 and includes content from the 30 seasons released over the years. What's more, all Champions - the game's hero characters - are unlocked for everyone to use, and most cosmetic items are available for all to equip too. Unfortunately, this transition also marks the end of ongoing development. "No additional content updates are planned at this time," id Software confirmed on Steam.
Quake Champions' new - and final - chapter kicks off with patch 1.31, and sees the removal of battle passes, the in-game store, paid currencies, loot boxes, login rewards, and all microtransactions. It also reorganises the UI to remove various free-to-play tabs and sections, with character customisation now more prominent on the main menu.
If you purchased Platinum within 60 days before 23rd September, you'll receive a refund. Additionally, anyone who's played Quake Champions previously on Steam will receive this updated, fully-featured version for free. The transition from the Microsoft Store "Xbox on PC" version is a little trickier, however. If you played before 23rd September and your Bethesda and Steam accounts are linked, you'll be given a Steam copy of Quake Champions within 48 hours, Bethesda confirmed. If your accounts weren't linked - or you didn't have a Steam account - you'll need to create one, sign into your Bethesda account, and link the two on this page. Your Steam copy should then arrive within 48 hours, but this can only be done until 7th October, so you have less than two weeks to do so.
Initially released in paid early access in 2017, Quake Champions was seen as something of a live-service experiment by id Software. It went free-to-play in 2018 and got its full release in 2022, following numerous updates which added new characters, weapons, and so many vanity items inspired by id Software's history.
Quake Champions never quite made the splash id expected it to. On Steam, the game peaked at 17,476 concurrent players (via SteamDB) when it first released. Lately, however, it's been hovering around 600 daily players. It also never came to consoles, which limited its potential audience further.

item.title: I'm not sure what's more surprising: that Xbox never had a Platinum Trophy equivalent, that Xbox feels the need to have a Platinum Trophy equivalent, or that it's adding a Platinum Trophy equivalent now while restructuring the company. Read more
item.description:
I'm not sure what's more surprising: that Xbox never had a Platinum Trophy equivalent, that Xbox feels the need to have a Platinum Trophy equivalent, or that it's adding a Platinum Trophy equivalent now while restructuring the company.
Nevertheless, that's what Microsoft appears to be doing. The Xbox PC App has reportedly been updated with a new Xbox Mythic Achievement that features an elaborate starred and laurelled symbol design, and an accompanying unlock sound that's 15-seconds long!
The update was spotted by reputable Xbox-watcher Klobrille, with website TrueAchievements adding that Mythic Achievements are worth zero Gamerscore and apparently retroactive. But there's no official confirmation of the Achievement yet, nor confirmation if it works exactly like a PlayStation Platinum Trophy - which is to say you earn it after earning every other Achievement or Trophy in a game. We've asked Microsoft for clarification.
A new update for the Xbox PC App reveals: Xbox Mythic Achievement; plus symbol and unlock sound.The Xbox Mythic Achievement is expected to be a 100% Gamerscore game completion reward. pic.twitter.com/STLisa4ubz
The Mythic naming, incidentally, is a nod to Halo's top-tier difficulty, although it's also a naming convention the Xbox-owned studio Blizzard has adopted across its wide roster of games to denote 'the absolute best thing' you can get, or challenge that you can face.
Speaking of Halo: Microsoft announced huge changes to the series this week when it revealed that Halo Studios was to all-but close and Halo development would move under the control of Activision - the publisher it bought for a colossal $68.7bn in 2023 - as part of a second wave of Xbox restructuring. Activision has "purpose-built" a new team, apparently, to develop the next Halo game.
It's a move that understandably has the Halo community concerned. Alongside questions around the next Halo Fest event, there's uncertainty around Activision plans for the future of the series. Especially given that, with Halo Studios' effective closure and the loss of so many jobs, the series loses a wealth of knowledge and experience.
Halo Studios wasn't the only casualty of the latest Xbox restructuring, with 268 jobs being lost in total across the division. Hellblade developer Ninja Theory is all-but closing after acquisition deals fell through; Age of Empires developer World's Edge reportedly lost half its team as it transitioned to Activision; RPG developer Obsidian moved under Bethesda's control, for better or worse; Forza (and Fable) developers Playground and Turn 10 were merged; and Rare moved under Activision as well. Our thoughts are with everyone affected by the lay-offs.

item.title: The times when a pair of pants prove newsworthy are tragically rare, and when they are it's usually not a good thing. Thankfully, a community discovery in World of Warcraft: Forever has remedied that. Read more
item.description:
The times when a pair of pants prove newsworthy are tragically rare, and when they are it's usually not a good thing. Thankfully, a community discovery in World of Warcraft: Forever has remedied that.
The Smelting Pants, discovered and posted to the World of Warcraft Classic Reddit, are a groundbreaking pair of trousers that could change the game's profession-related crafting forever.
A rare drop from a currently unknown location, these leather pantaloons provide boosts in both Stamina and Spirit. More importantly, though, they reduce the smelting time of copper, tin, bronze, and silver by a whopping 25 percent.
This may not sound like a big deal, but it has major ramifications for the wider release of World of Warcraft: Forever. In Classic WoW - the unaltered vanilla WoW experience - no gear with profession boosts like this exists, signalling game-changing intent on the behalf of Blizzard, and much needed help for those focusing on professions in Forever's full release.
A somewhat similar system is in place in the modern version of World of Warcraft. In recent expansions, profession equipment has been added that provides boosts to crafting and gathering skills. However, these differ in that they are mostly crafted using the profession system, rather than being a drop from something in the wider world.
There have been items in Classic WoW that boosted skills, such as fancier fishing rods, however those only offered boosts to your overall profession level. The Smelting Pants are altogether different: the bonuses to smelting time are unrivaled in pre-existing Classic WoW equipment, garments or otherwise.
The reactions to this Reddit trouser-post are as delighted and playful as you might expect. MaleficentBank405 wrote: "Fantastic pants", while LeWigre responded: "I love this kind of stuff. Not everything has to improve your character, some things can just be fun or pretty to get!" HighWalker321 put it more simply: "I call these my hot pants."
Who knew a pair of pants could be so exciting? It's one example of the deluge of unexpected new things players are discovering in the World of Warcraft: Forever beta. Whether this sort of treasure exists later on in the game's more treacherous locales is something we'll have to find out, come Forever's full release on 4th November.

item.title: After announcing the end of Destiny 2 development and laying off almost the game's entire team, Bungie surprised fans earlier this week with news that it's working on "unvaulting" Destiny 2 campaigns, raids and destinations - bringing them back to the game after they were removed. The developer offered few specifics at the time, but new information has now emerged about what we can expect. Read more
item.description:
After announcing the end of Destiny 2 development and laying off almost the game's entire team, Bungie surprised fans earlier this week with news that it's working on "unvaulting" Destiny 2 campaigns, raids and destinations - bringing them back to the game after they were removed. The developer offered few specifics at the time, but new information has now emerged about what we can expect.
The information comes from a Forbes report where reporter Paul Tassi attempted to answer those lingering questions using their sources inside Bungie. According to Tassi, all unvaulted game additions are going to be free for everyone, including those who did not own them originally. Indeed, as Tassie pointed out, much of the stuff had already been made free-to-play before it went away.
But though the campaigns, raids and destinations are coming back, the live service seasons that ran alongside them are not, which is partially to be expected, seeing as seasons are transient in nature. In Destiny 2's case, however, some of those seasons included story additions that set up future expansions, so there may be some gaps in storytelling.
Seasonal events are likewise not included in the unvaulting, partly because the weapons they introduced are already in the game. As Tassi noted, many players would prefer it if the game cycled through seasonal events, but that would require a Destiny 2 live-ops team that no longer exists.
There's also the matter of activities some of those seasons introduced to the game. According to the report, there's no indication they will return, but Tassi didn't rule out the possibility of some of them returning as standalone activities at some point. They further pointed out that you probably shouldn't expect every Strike, Crucible or Gambit map to return, though the chances are higher for Strikes that have narrative hooks, as they'd be considered part of the story.
Nevertheless, the report confirmed what many had suspected reading Bungie's announcement: this unvaulting doesn't mean the studio is returning to regular Destiny 2 development. No more patches are to be released between now and the unvaulting, save for any that address major bugs - as originally planned.
"Monument of Triumph really was end-of-service for the live part of Destiny 2," Tassi wrote. "As you may recall, almost everyone managing Destiny was laid off."
As for when the unvaulting is expected to arrive, Tassi couldn't say for certain, though their guess is "sometime next year". Until then, expect things to go quiet again on the Destiny 2 front, though a big Marathon update is expected in December.

item.title: Discord delayed the rollout of its controversial age verification system back in February after very loud backlash against the company's plans. Those age checks are now back, but this time, co-founder and chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy says the updated system will give users options that aren't as invasive. Read more
item.description:
Discord delayed the rollout of its controversial age verification system back in February after very loud backlash against the company's plans. Those age checks are now back, but this time, co-founder and chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy says the updated system will give users options that aren't as invasive.
Near the start of the year, Discord's age checks planned to automatically give all users a "teen-appropriate experience" by blurring potentially "sensitive content" or restricting access to age-gated channels. Getting rid of the blocks would have required users to verify their age by submitting a photo of their government-issued ID or a video recording of their face to one of the platform's third-party vendors. As you can imagine, Discord users weren't thrilled about sharing sensitive data like that.
"Age assurance draws strong opinions and scepticism, especially when it involves sharing biometric information or a form of ID," Vishnevskiy said in a new blog post. "At the same time, age assurance laws are expanding, and since my last post we've had to launch age assurance in other regions, including in Brazil and in Texas. We're hearing from policymakers in countless states and countries who want stronger teen protections, from the European Union to Indonesia. To me, that makes it more important than ever to show that this can be done in a privacy-preserving way: one where more than 90% of you won’t have to confirm your age."
The new age verification system, rolling out over the course of this week for everyone, will automatically guess a user's age based on how long an account's been around for or the types of servers they're involved in. "We don't look at your messages, calls, or other content," Vishnevskiy promised.
If Discord automatically places an account in the 18+ adult range, nothing will change. Users placed in the teens (13-17) age group will have "additional safety protections that block age-restricted content, spaces, and setting." If you're an adult who hasn't been recognised as an adult by Discord, there'll be more "non-biometric" ways of verifying how old you are.
"We've vetted every method, and the data you provide to us and our vendors is only ever used to determine your age group, so you can pick whichever option you're most comfortable with," Vishnevskiy added. You can now input your credit card info or allow the Apple App Store/Google Play Store to share an age rating with Discord, for example. A more comprehensive list is available on Vishnevskiy's statement.
"Any form of age assurance, and the possibility of sharing something biometric or an ID, is a controversial topic. Rightfully so, because of what it represents and where internet legislation around the world is heading: toward a more gated internet. This is bigger than us," Vishnevskiy continued. "We've chosen to launch our stronger protections for teens everywhere using the most privacy-preserving approach we could build, including where it isn't yet required by law, because we believe it's the right thing to do. By launching a global approach with non-biometric options, we're getting ahead of laws that might ask us to implement something less privacy-focused. The decisions policymakers make now will shape how platforms advance both teen safety and privacy for years to come, and I encourage people to make their perspectives heard where they live."

item.description:
UPDATE 25/09/26: Halo Studios' esports lead has confirmed December's Halo Fest lives on, despite layoffs sweeping through the rest of the developer. Further updates about the live event might take a little while to come our way as the studio is busy providing "support and care for our teammates," understandably. I've left the full statement below.
"Jumping on here briefly to confirm Halo Fest is still on for December. No changes to dates, locations, etc. For more details on the event, I'm going to please ask for your patience as our first priority is to provide support and care for our teammates. We will communicate more updates in the coming weeks," the series' esports lead wrote on social media.
ORIGINAL STORY: We're now living in a timeline that would have been impossible to comprehend for a grunt-squashing teen in 2007: Activision is making the next Halo game. And, now, fans have questions about the change. Is this year's Halo Fest still happening, despite sweeping layoffs at Halo Studios? Will Activision's new game reboot the lore? Can Master Chief finally, please, catch a break?
"We are eliminating 268 roles across Halo Studios, other first-party studios, and the XGS management and central functions layer," Xbox Studios chief Matt Booty wrote in a statement this week as part of the console maker's wide-ranging restructure. "Activision will also be developing the next Halo title, led by a new, purpose-built team that is separate from ongoing development and plans for Call of Duty. A small team at Halo Studios will continue supporting the Halo community and games in-market."
Xbox's restructuring laid off 1,600 workers this summer, with a further 1,600 job cuts planned over the course of the year, but it also rejigged several studios. Obsidian is now part of Bethesda, for example, and Halo is now part of Activision, along with Rare and World's Edge.
It's a dramatic shift for a franchise that was once Xbox's golden goose, and fans are conflicted about what it means for the future of the iconic sci-fi shooter series. One big worry is Activision may reboot the story and throw away lore that's been built up across 25 years - or, perhaps, scrap some of the extended universe lore, as Disney did to Star Wars when it took over that galaxy.
Honestly that’s my biggest fear. I fear that they’ll just do a general reset on Halo’s established lore.If that happens, I’m out https://t.co/SkpENQih3u
Frankly I'm out if they DON'T do a semi-reboot and axe ALL of 343's lore. There is zero future for any stories which share a continuity with Halo 4, 5, and Infinite. https://t.co/ti32iP4qBv
gotta love how the mass resetting of Halo as well as a FULL reboot is happening right after the franchise left off on a blank fucking canvas. Ripe for any possibilities. Backwards company. https://t.co/WV0TqHXPuA
Hot take, but I want Activision to reboot Halo back to just after Halo 3, no 343 Forerunner lore, and focus on a war story about humanity rebuilding and parts of the galaxy resisting that.Halo has strayed too far from humanity while trying to make Chief human, ironically.
"That would be another terrible idea in a string of terrible ideas," one Redditor wrote in response to a rumor suggesting Activision's Halo is, in fact, a reboot. "Doubtful tbh. Restarting after Halo 3 maybe at most," another said. The duality of man, I guess?
Another big question mark hangs over Halo Fest Seattle, which was scheduled to celebrate the series' 25th anniversary with fans in December. There's been lots of speculation these past few days about whether the live event goes ahead, considering most of Halo Studios has been gutted.
In a statement given to Kotaku, Activision president Rob Kostich said the company's goal is to "make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place." Kostich's statement is certainly vague enough that things could go either way - it sounds like whatever studio ends up taking over the series hasn't even been assembled yet, so discussions about lore probably won't happen for quite some time. Regardless, binning two decades worth of stories and really cool world building seems like a big shame. There's still so much untapped material in the novels that's ripe for a video game adaptation, akin to Halo Reach, as well.
And, I agree with a faction of the Halo community, parts of the post-Bungie era were a mess - messy to follow as a player without reading every published Halo book and, probably, messy for a developer trying to figure out a sensible path forward. But Halo Infinite ended with a clean slate, of sorts. Cortana 1.0 is gone, a new threat is on the horizon, and all the space magic nonsense has seemingly been forgotten about. Why start from scratch, again?

item.title: Xbox's massive and still ongoing reorganisation has pushed Obsidian Entertainment under Bethesda's umbrella. Despite the quite drastic corporate shakeup, Bethesda's president is promising folks the iconic RPG developer will hold onto its "creative identity." Read more
item.description:
Xbox's massive and still ongoing reorganisation has pushed Obsidian Entertainment under Bethesda's umbrella. Despite the quite drastic corporate shakeup, Bethesda's president is promising folks the iconic RPG developer will hold onto its "creative identity."
Xbox's so-called "reset" kicked off earlier this year with the console maker laying off 1,600 workers and parting ways with five first-party developers. This week's continuation saw a further 268 roles cut across the division, and plenty of studios have moved around Microsoft's various gaming divisions as a result. Halo, Rare (Sea of Thieves) and World's Edge (Age of Empires) are now under Activision's control, while Obsidian Entertainment is being folded into Bethesda - all of them used to fall under the Xbox Game Studios banner.
While some fans are worried Obsidian might be downgraded to a mere support studio - it's currently developing a new Fallout game with Bethesda Game Studios, after all - Bethesda president Jill Braff told employees there's not much to worry about.
"The creative identity and strengths that make Obsidian distinct will remain at the core of their studio and work," Braff said in an email to staff, according to a copy seen by Aftermath. "[CEO Feargus Urquhart] and the Obsidian leadership team will continue to lead Obsidian, with the studio reporting to me. Bethesda Game Studios will continue to lead the Fallout franchise. Together, the teams will build on their longstanding relationship and the early work already underway on a new Fallout project, with more to share in the months ahead. This structure supports the franchise-led model we've been strengthening while keeping accountability for both the studio and the franchise clear."
In Xbox's first round of mass layoffs this summer, the famed role-playing powerhouse reportedly lost around 25% of its workforce and had to cancel several in-development projects. The above "franchise-led model" seems to have been the reason why. Former Xbox leadership took an oddly hands-free approach to many of its in-house developers, but new CEO Asha Sharma has been more forthcoming about her desire to focus on the firm's biggest of big names - The Elder Scrolls, Halo, Fallout, etc. Many of Obsidian's original games this generation, including Avowed and The Outer Worlds 2, apparently underperformed, perhaps explaining why it's now back playing in Fallout's radioactive wasteland.

item.title: As if this season wasn't packed enough with games to play, the acclaimed 'Nemesis system' Lord of the Rings games Shadow of Mordor and Shadow of War finally come to Switch 2 later this month. Read more
item.description:
As if this season wasn't packed enough with games to play, the acclaimed 'Nemesis system' Lord of the Rings games Shadow of Mordor and Shadow of War finally come to Switch 2 later this month.
Set to launch on the console on the 30th September, both Lord of the Rings games boast all previously released DLC. Aspyr seems to have handled the conversions, and both games are available in a new bundle that you can pre-order for 50 percent off. Without the discount, the bundle sells for £62.99 / $70.
In Eurogamer's Shadow of Mordor review from 2015, Aoife Wilson - like so many other people - praised the game's procedural Nemesis system, whereby the game's enemies could level up after encounters with you and rise through their own ranks. This system helped make an otherwise passable open-world action games feel refreshing. Johnny Chiodini reviewed Shadow of War in 2017, but felt that improved gameplay was let down by a dreadful story.
The Nemesis system has remained a standout feature from the series. Aside from a few exceptions, like the Lich system in Warframe and maybe Watch Dogs: Legion's NPC relationship system, few other games have implemented something similar. Perhaps that's because Warner Bros owns the patent until 2036.
Aspyr recently remastered ropy old Lord of the Rings game War in the North, suggesting at the time it wouldn't be the last "classic" LOTR game re-released. Are there even more to come, I wonder? Sadly, as for entirely new games from Monolith, the studio closed in 2025, with an in-development Wonder Woman game cancelled as a result.

item.title: Blizzard has hinted at yet another core mechanic in Diablo 5 seemingly inspired by Diablo 2. Notably, the in-development action-RPG will tackle level-scaling differently from the way it's done in Diablo 4. Read more
item.description:
Blizzard has hinted at yet another core mechanic in Diablo 5 seemingly inspired by Diablo 2. Notably, the in-development action-RPG will tackle level-scaling differently from the way it's done in Diablo 4.
Game director Joe Shely revealed - in a roundtable interview at BlizzCon (via PC Gamer) - that Blizzard is aware of the desire to feel powerful in Diablo games, a feeling that the level-scaling system in Diablo 4 (and 3) somewhat betrays.
If you're unfamiliar, automatic level scaling is when enemies in a game's world keep pace with your own level. In other words, you're never going to run into an area where enemies out level you, but similarly you can't go back to the starting zone and feel how much more powerful you've become. This was the approach adopted by Diablos 3 and 4 - a somewhat controversial change from Diablo 2.
Said Shely: "Diablo is a game that, in many ways, is about your character getting stronger and when the monsters get stronger at the same time, especially outside of your control… You've filled the experience bar, you get stronger, you should feel awesome now: a wave of light pulses out from you, a bunch of monsters die."
"And sometimes automatic scaling can get in the way of that feeling," Shely added, "which is so core to it, and that's why this is a really important question. And so, we're going to take a somewhat different approach to that in Diablo 5."
As to what that different approach will look like, Shely wouldn't say, but did admit the team hasn't fully discussed level-scaling yet.
That said, this is a clear indication that Blizzard is at least willing to toy around with the idea of changing a core system that's been used by two successive Diablo games. And this isn't the only Diablo 2-inspired mechanic: Blizzard previously said Diablo 5's itemisation and loot - including more complex inventory-management - are also inspired by Diablo 2.
In fact, looking at everything we've learned so far about Diablo 5, it's clear Blizzard is aiming for a more demanding experience, favouring the sort of player-friction and challenge that ARPG rival games Path of Exile 1 and 2 are known for - and that Diablo used to be known for.
However, there's quite a wait before we see how many of those design ideas manifest in the final game: Diablo 5 isn't due for release until spring 2029.

item.title: Former Halo leaders Bonnie Ross and Kiki Wolfkill have added their voices to the chorus of people wishing laid-off Halo Studios employees well after Microsoft's drastic downsizing of the studio yesterday. Read more
item.description:
Former Halo leaders Bonnie Ross and Kiki Wolfkill have added their voices to the chorus of people wishing laid-off Halo Studios employees well after Microsoft's drastic downsizing of the studio yesterday.
The Xbox cuts were so sudden one former Halo Studios employee, cinematic director Josh Daniels, said he was promoted and then laid off in the same week. "Promoted and laid off in the same week is pretty wild," wrote Daniels on LinkedIn. "I'm one of the many hit by the Halo Studios layoffs."
Daniels' departure was a result of yesterday's Xbox cuts, which saw 268 people lose their jobs across a combination of Halo Studios, other unnamed first-party studios, and Xbox Game Studios management layers.
Halo Studios is reduced to a "small" support team as a result, with major Halo development moving to Activision, where a "purpose-built" team - separate from Call of Duty - has been created to develop "the next Halo title".
Bonnie Ross, the former head of Halo and founder of 343 Industries (which became Halo Studios), responded to yesterday's news on LinkedIn: "It was difficult to wake up to the news that the Halo Studio is essentially being shut down today, with only a small number of roles remaining," she wrote.
"Hundreds of incredibly talented team members are being impacted with creatives, designers, engineers, producers, artists, narrative and audio specialists, data insights, ops, community leaders and franchise teams who poured their passion into Halo, gaming, and engaging and serving players and fans.
"My thoughts are with every Halo team member and with the broader Xbox teams affected. For teams looking to hire, you will not find a more dedicated, capable, or community-driven group of people. Their talent and heart run deep."
Kiki Wolfkill, another enormously influential figure in Halo's recent history, having led 343 Studios for a number of years, added that she was "gutted to hear the news today". "Sending love and support to everyone impacted by the layoffs at Halo Studios and across Xbox. I know how much talent, heart, and care these teams pour into this work—and how deeply this can affect individuals, families, and teams.
"If I can be helpful in any way—making an introduction, offering advice, being a sounding board, or simply listening—please, please reach out. My door is open."
Exactly how many people at Halo Studios have been let go, we don't officially know, though there are unconfirmed reports - such as one on Windows Central - that layoffs are in their hundreds. LinkedIn has a lot of Halo Studios-related posts, and a few offer some clues about the extent of the cuts.
One former employee said they, "along with the majority of Halo Studios", were laid off yesterday, while another former employee said "Halo Studios 'shut down' today".
343 Industries was created in 2007 after Halo series creator Bungie bought back its independence, and it has developed or overseen development of every Halo game since Halo: Reach in 2010. The studio was rebranded as Halo Studios two years ago.
Yesterday's Xbox cuts also resulted in what appears to be the impending closure of British studio Ninja Theory, as well as organisational changes, as Obsidian moves under Bethesda's control, Playground and Turn 10 merge, Undead Labs goes independent, and Rare, World's Edge and Halo move under Activision's control. So far, it's emerged that Undead Labs has also suffered major layoffs as a result, as well as Age of Empires and Mythology developer World's Edge.

item.title: Shift UP CEO Hyung-Tae Kim has spoken about the troubles faced during Stellar Blade's development, including doubts from investors about the game's ability to break even, and rapidly depleting funds to pay staff with. Read more
item.description:
Shift UP CEO Hyung-Tae Kim has spoken about the troubles faced during Stellar Blade's development, including doubts from investors about the game's ability to break even, and rapidly depleting funds to pay staff with.
Speaking to Korean gaming outlet Inven (translated into English with Google Translate), Kim said: "During the development of Stellar Blade there was a time when the company was in a situation where it could only pay salaries for about three months."
Kim went on to explain that Shift Up visited various investors to secure financial support for Stellar Blade's development, only to be told it was too risky. Many asked why they were making the game when "it was obvious it would not break even", and Kim claimed he was told that if they pursued a different project the company would be valued more.
Kim had his own doubts at the time, apparently."There were times when I questioned whether it was truly right to make a game like this in Korea," he said. "However, we somehow managed to develop it to the end, and it was the users' choices that proved the path we had chosen was not wrong."
Thankfully for Kim and Shift Up, Stellar Blade proved quite the success. While exact console figures are unknown, it sold millions of copies on PS5 and later was a record-breaking release on PC, breaking 1m sales within three days. Shift Up is currently working on the sequel Stellar Blade: Blood Rain, which has yet to receive a release date.
It's a nice story, especially given the wider context of South Korea's rising presence in the triple-A development space in recent years. Another Korean developer that also found big success recently was Pearl Abyss, with Crimson Desert, which sold exceptionally well as well.

item.description:
Yesterday's Xbox cuts saw organisational restructuring that moved Age of Empires studio World's Edge under Activision's control. The initial announcement did not specify whether the Age of Empire studio would lose any staff as part of this transition, but new information has emerged suggesting many members of the team have been let go.
According to former creative director Adam Isgreen, World's Edge lost nearly half of its staff in the Xbox restructuring and Activision transition. Isgreen revealed this in a post on the Resetera forums (via VGChartz). Under the (verified) username Tempus Chaoti, he wrote: "What a morning. FYI World's Edge was not spared completely - just under half the studio was let go - myself included. Been fun, y'all!"
In a follow-up post on LinkedIn, Isgreen, who spent over 16 years at Microsoft in various positions, listed a number of projects he was part of, including Windows Phone, Xbox Live Arcade, and the games Ori, Minecraft, Trials HD, State of Decay, Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet, World of Tanks and "many, many more".
Isgreen also apparently helped publish games such as Recore, Killer Instinct, Fable, Crackdown, and of course the Age of Empires franchises "and all the great games and expansions we released throughout the years".
"I didn't think I'd be working on RTS games again years after their first 'heyday', but am I ever proud of what our studio team and partners were able to do with the series and juice the genre's return," Isgreen wrote. "I think the fans would agree (mostly!) that we delivered the goods for all of 'em."
"I am of course disappointed that this is the way the time with World's Edge and Age [of Empires] ends for myself and many of my talented teammates that were also impacted," Isgreen added. "We had some great plans for what's next - and I hope the team that remains can rise to the occasion down the line."
Yesterday's Xbox cuts resulted in the impending closure of Ninja Theory, the Halo franchise moving to Activision and Halo Studios all-but closing because of it, Playground and Turn10 merging, Obsidian moving under Bethesda's control, and Rare moving under Activision's control as well.
Many questions remain about the full impact of these transitions and whether - not to put too blunt a point on it - it will work. Our thoughts are with everyone affected by the layoffs.

item.title: Star Wars Zero Company, the XCOM-like turn-based tactics game from Bit Reactor, appears to have been a success, selling more than 1m copies, according to estimates from industry analyst Alinea Analytics. Read more
item.description:
Star Wars Zero Company, the XCOM-like turn-based tactics game from Bit Reactor, appears to have been a success, selling more than 1m copies, according to estimates from industry analyst Alinea Analytics.
It's a notable achievement for Star Wars Zero Company, but the sales milestone is especially pertinent against the backdrop of "most" of Bit Reactor's development team being furloughed without pay before the game's release. This was reportedly a consequence of a dispute between the studio's owners, as well as a lack of funds, so it raises the question now of whether the team will be reinstated and paid using revenue generated by sales of the game.
Star Wars Zero Company's most successful platform has been Steam, with a dominating 69.9 percent of copies sold, followed by 19.9 percent on PlayStation and 10.2 percent on Xbox - including copies sold through Xbox on PC.
Alinea's Rhys Elliott estimated that Zero Company made about $50m (~£37m) in revenue since it launched on 27th August, which he said is "respectable for this genre and during such a crowded period (even with the Star Wars brand attached)".
Incidentally, while Zero Company sold fewer copies on console, it made more money per person there, simply because, as Elliott noted: "Console players pay more per copy."
The overwhelming majority of Zero Company's audience - 90 percent - is split between North America and Europe, with only five percent in Asia, according to Alinea's breakdown. Perhaps that's a reflection of Star Wars' own popularity in the world. Zero Company's success also puts it in the top-five-earning games of 2026 based on a major intellectual property (IP). The biggest earning, by some margin, is James Bond game 007 First Light, with $309.8m (~£233m). Zero Company is only the latest of recently-released games to cross the million sales milestone. The Blood of Dawnwalker and Onimusha: Way of the Sword were both released around the same time and have each sold over a million copies.
We haven't reviewed Star Wars Zero Company yet, but are working on it. However, Christian Donlan wrote enthusiastically about the game after a few hours with it, saying: "Star Wars Zero Company understands that Star Wars games should feel less like the movies and more like the toys."

item.title: The story director for Gears of War: E-Day has been laid off as part of yesterday's Xbox cuts, barely two weeks before the game he's worked on for more than four years is released. Read more
item.description:
The story director for Gears of War: E-Day has been laid off as part of yesterday's Xbox cuts, barely two weeks before the game he's worked on for more than four years is released.
Juan Vaca, who joined Gears of War: E-Day developer Coalition in 2022, announced he had been laid off from the company on LinkedIn last night. Vaca wrote: "I am part of this round of Microsoft layoffs and am open to new opportunities in games/film/tv. If your team needs a director/storyteller please reach out."
Vaca's prior post, made only five days ago, was a celebration of Gears of War: E-Day going gold (meaning the game is ready to be printed on discs). The game itself is set to be released on 6th October.
It is uncertain how many more developers at The Coalition, if any, have been impacted by this wave of Xbox cuts. According to Kotaku, which spoke to an anonymous source familiar with the situation, fewer than "a handful" of developers were laid off, and for reasons apparently unrelated to Xbox restructuring.
Yesterday was another day of upheaval for Xbox, with multiple studios consolidated or drastically altered as a result of ongoing restructuring work. 268 developers were laid off in total. Studios Rare and World's Edge were moved under Activision's control, Playground and Turn 10 will merge into one studio focused on Fable and Forza, and Obsidian - which is making a new Fallout game - now reports into Bethesda.
On top of that, Halo Studios has been drastically downsized as part of these layoffs, with Halo series development moving to Activision for future releases. Finally, Ninja Theory is heading towards closure, after potential new ownership deals fell through.

item.description:
There's a bit somewhere in the middle of the rubbish Doom movie, where the perspective suddenly switches to first-person. Look, it seems to say, it's just like you playing the video game! But what Zach Cregger's new Resident Evil movie gets is that, really, it's nothing like me playing the video game. Back on my side of the screen, I might be sitting in a digital space marine suit, gliding around gloomy corridors as monsters leap at my face, but I'm certainly not behaving like one. I am shrieking; I am cringing, I am swearing; I am fumbling the controller, and I'm firing stray bullets at the roof. And while, yes, I might occasionally allow myself a quick celebrity whoop, the power fantasy is hardly a total one.
That, I think, is what makes Cregger's movie take on Resident Evil so enormously fun. It perfectly captures that relatable joy of video game cack-handedness, the laughable errors of judgement, the misplaced overconfidence, and, ultimately, the can-do spirit that, usually, just about carries us through. Here, our player stand-in is Bryan, a charismatically rumpled medical courier and everyman (wonderfully played by Austin Abrams), who finds himself embroiled in Raccoon City's T-virus outbreak one unfortunate snowy evening.
It's a journey that begins in a busy hospital and ends, as is series tradition, in a corporate lab, taking in a whole bunch of other familiar Resident Evil touchpoints - an eerily abandoned farmhouse, the city's zombie-infected streets, a brief detour down into the sewers - along the way. Creggers also structures his movie like a video game; he sends Bryan forth on a plot-light, action-heavy misadventure that - after his initial quest is set - plays out more or less in real-time, merrily bouncing from enemy encounter to set-piece to boss fight and back again. He even gets some drawer-rifling ammo-hunting in.
Throughout it all, Bryan pluckily bumbles his way forward with resigned - and, in a winning bit of characterisation, obliviously selfless - determination, monologuing near continuously with a stream of 'fucks' and 'shits'. Oh, and fear-racked gargles so exotic, I'm fairly certain they constitute entirely new sounds. As someone who just spent the last week playing Silent Hill: Townfall, emitting a very similar stream of vocal diarrhea, I can't tell you how wonderful it is to be so accurately represented on screen.
In the wrong hands, this kind of metatextual approach would suck, but Cregger - who co-wrote the script with Shay Hatten - is unquestionably the right man for the job. He's already proven his horror and comedy chops in the marvellous Barbarian and Weapons, and his distinctive sensibilities serve Resident Evil (a series perpetually operating in the register of camp, even if it's managed to do it with a straighter face in recent times) extremely well. As much as I adore the games and their pantheon of high-cheekboned heroes, their silly stories are B-movie at best, and I'm more than happy for someone to have a bit of fun with the series on the big screen.
And Cregger's Resident Evil is so much fun, swinging wildly from jumpscares and genuine tension to slapstick ludicrousness in a way that, while still unmistakably Cregger, can't help but bring Sam Raimi to mind. Raimi's Drag Me to Hell is, I reckon, the pinnacle of horror-comedy, and a masterful display of horror tension management as it constantly undercuts its scare gags with actual gags then undercuts those in turn, each switch amplifying the impact of the next one. By comparison, Cregger's Resident Evil leans far harder into gross-out comedy than straight-up horror, but it still finds a rhythm that helps each half land harder. And there are plenty of moments that hit that sweet spot, stranding you somewhere between incredulous laugh and strangled gasp when they come (hi dog!).
Resident Evil might be running on the flimsiest of plots, but that balance, Abrams' endlessly likeable presence, some silly running gags, and a succession of stellar set-pieces keeps it buzzing along. And as far as the latter goes, Resident Evil has some treats. It's got roly poly creatures that give Arcadian's horsey horrors a run for their money, a supremely silly car runaround, the world's worst elevator ride, and a breathlessly orchestrated zombie rainstorm that still impresses, even if you did have it spoiled by the trailer (I really should've learned my lesson by now). Honestly, it's hard to pick a favourite. And throughout, those brilliantly gloopy body horror monstrosities: mostly new creations, but perfectly Resident Evil all the same.
What I'm saying is I had a great time. Cregger's Resident Evil film might not be every fan's cup of tea with its abundant silliness, its slender throughline, and its lack of Leon, Claire, et al, but it's easily the best video game adaptation of playing a video game I've seen. And in its daft subversiveness - in doggedly, wisely sticking to the periphery of the Resident Evil series' wider world - I think Cregger also captures the spirit of his source material better than most other game-to-movie adaptations do. As Bryan puts it at one point in a rare moment of triumph: "Video gaaaaaaaames!"

item.title: State of Decay studio Undead Labs has shared good and bad news following Xbox's second round of job cuts this year. Read more
item.description:
State of Decay studio Undead Labs has shared good and bad news following Xbox's second round of job cuts this year.
The good news is that Undead Labs, owned by Microsoft since 2018, has gone independent and is worker-owned as well, the studio said in a statement on its website. The bad news is that the studio is laying off "a significant number" of staff in doing so, the company added on LinkedIn.
"Independence brings us closer to our community and lets us focus on what matters most: making the best games we can and earning the continued support of the people who choose to spend their time with us," Undead Labs studio head Philip Holt said in the website statement.
"Unfortunately," Undead Labs added on LinkedIn, "today we are also saying goodbye to a significant number of our colleagues. It's difficult to reach this moment knowing that not everyone who helped get us here gets to make the rest of the journey with us.
"There have been far too many announcements like this across the industry, and we hate adding to that list. These are people we'd hire again in a heartbeat, and we hope the industry takes notice."
Undead Labs was one of the studios Xbox said it was parting with when Microsoft announced the beginning of its restructuring this summer. At the time, Microsoft said it had found a buyer for the studio, but didn't name them. Microsoft also said a similar thing about Ninja Theory, another studio it previously owned, though it announced yesterday that it may have to close the studio after two deals fell through.
State of Decay 3 remains in development, and the studio reiterated its aim for the game to enter closed beta before the end of the year, with 2027 remaining as the release target. State of Decay 3 also remains a Game Pass game, Xbox Studios boss Matt Booty wrote in his message to staff about restructuring yesterday. There had been concern the game wouldn't launch into Game Pass post-separation.
Booty's message also said State of Decay 3 has a new publisher, though once again did not name them. It's also in development for PC and PlayStation, alongside Xbox.
Undead Labs' separation from Xbox brings a 15-year partnership to an end. Xbox published the charming if scrappy zombie survival game State of Decay in 2013, before acquiring the studio in 2018 mere days after State of Decay 2 was released - a sequel we didn't like at all.

item.description:
If you're an enjoyer of video game maps, you might like this: celebrated artist and cartographer Francesca Baerald - who's created in-game (and out) maps for Dragon Age, Warcraft, Octopath Traveler, Diablo, Dungeons & Dragons and many more - is releasing a glossy new art book. It's an oversized, A3 book that features page after page of her sumptuously detailed, hand-painted maps.
Unbound - The Cartography Art Book by Francesca Baerald, as it's known, is currently being crowdfunded. But it's already a huge success on Kickstarter, having raised more than four times its £20k goal with weeks to spare. The book includes more than 250 maps from Baerald's work in video games, tabletop RPGs, board games, and graphic novels.
If Baerald's name is familiar, it might be because I talked to her for a long piece I wrote about the creation of game maps a couple of years ago. What I found especially intriguing about her work was that Baerald creates maps almost exclusively physically, by painting in watercolour, rather than using digital software to create them.
"I believe a perfect map should inspire players and readers from the first glance," Baerald told me at the time. "I see maps not as instruments to find directions in a game, but as decorated, welcoming doorways that drag you into the game's world."
The book is expensive at €150 for a Standard Edition (€250 for a Premium Edition, and €2000 for a wonderfully lavish-sounding Limited Edition, hand-bound in Italy using ancient techniques at a book-binder called Bottega dei Gozzi). But there's an emphasis on the book's size and the quality of the prints and paper within it. It's said to be 99 percent finished, too, although copies won't ship until next summer.
